title: Hosted API Demo - Chat & Text Generation Basics (Synergy AI)
summary: Intro demo of Redwood Hosted API focusing on chat/text generation basics: streaming responses, core parameters (temperature, max_tokens, top_p), retry behavior and idempotency, and basic cost/latency trade-offs. Customer is evaluating hosted vs dedicated for production; interested in security (SOC2, KMS, VPC options) and a short pilot/benchmarks.
topics: Overview of Hosted API endpoints (chat, text generation, streaming)
Parameters and sampling: temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop sequences
Streaming best practices and partial response handling
Retries, idempotency tokens, and exponential backoff
Latency vs cost trade-offs; batching/caching mentions
Security/enterprise: SOC 2, SSO, KMS, VPC/Private deployment options
Next steps: pricing, security docs, trial account and benchmark run
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-22
Start: 16:00 PDT
Duration: ~47 min
Attendees: Maya Chen (AE, Redwood), Jon Patel (SE, Redwood), Liam O'Connor (Synergy AI), Priya Rao (Synergy), Evan Miles (Synergy)

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone thanks for joining; I'm Maya from Redwood Inference, and with me is Jon our solutions engineer. How's everybody doing?
[00:07] Liam O'Connor: Good thanks. Excited to see the hosted api stuff — we wanna understand streaming and how retries work.
[00:12] Maya Chen: Perfect. We'll do a quick architecture overview then jump into a live demo: chat and text generation endpoints, streaming, params like temperature/top_p, and retry/idempotency patterns.
[00:25] Jon Patel: Quick note, I'll show the Console and then run an API call from a notebook. There may be a couple of typos in the transcript — audio auto transcribed.

[02:00] Jon Patel: Okay first, the chat endpoint is basically a structured messages format: role user/system/assistant, and you can stream partial tokens as they generate. For streaming we support SSE and streaming HTTP — you can pipe partial deltas to your client.
[02:22] Priya Rao: Is streaming guaranteed in order? We have a web UI that displays tokens as they arrive.
[02:28] Jon Patel: Usually yes; tokens are ordered. There can be small reorders if you run multi-shard requests but default hosted is single-shard for low-latency chat.

[04:10] Liam O'Connor: Walk us through params — we have a real-time chat product so latency matters and we tune sampling aggressively.
[04:18] Jon Patel: Sure. Key params: temperature (0-1 typically), top_p (nucleus sampling), max_tokens, stop sequences. Lower temperature reduces variance and can speed up generation slightly because of shorter beams on some runtimes; but main latency wins are sequence length and model size.
[04:45] Jon Patel: Also mention top_k if you want deterministic-ish truncation; not all models need top_k. We also have presence/ frequency penalties if you want to discourage repeats.

[06:30] Evan Miles: How do you handle rate limits and retries? If a token stream fails mid-way what do we do?
[06:38] Maya Chen: Good question. For transient failures we recommend retries with idempotency tokens for non-streaming calls. For streaming we recommend a short resume: either re-request from last assistant message or buffer partial tokens client-side and reconnect.
[06:58] Jon Patel: Our SDKs include a retry helper; default is exponential backoff with jitter. For safety you should be using an idempotency key for any request that modifies state or for cost accounting.

[09:15] Priya Rao: Any advice for partial-response UX so we avoid duplicates when reconnecting?
[09:23] Jon Patel: Keep the last confirmed assistant token index on the client, then on reconnect ask the model to continue given the conversation prior to that token. If you need exact dedupe, use message hashes.

[11:40] Liam O'Connor: Let's demo. Jon, can you show a streaming chat with temperature adjustments?
[11:46] Jon Patel: Yeah — opening the Console. (brief typing sounds) Here's a chat call with model: redwood/gpt-3.5-like (note: model names transcribed slightly off). First call: temperature 0.7, max_tokens 150, stream=true.
[12:10] [live demo output streaming tokens appears]
[12:40] Jon Patel: You can see partial tokens flowing. If I drop temperature to 0.2 you get more conservative answers, and the stream finishes a bit quicker in practice because responses are shorter.

[15:05] Evan Miles: How do you measure cost? Per-token? We have strict budget constraints.
[15:12] Maya Chen: Hosted API is billed per input/output token; we show token-level cost breakdown in the Console. For production you can enable prefix caching and batching to reduce per-token cost. Dedicated customers can get different unit economics.

[17:00] Priya Rao: Caching — is it safe for PII? We can't cache sensitive user data.
[17:07] Jon Patel: By default, hosted can be opted-out of caching per request. For sensitive data you can set no_cache=true and enable encryption at rest with KMS. If you require tenant isolation we can discuss Dedicated or Private deployments.

[19:30] Liam O'Connor: Security items: SOC 2, SSO, KMS — what's available out of the box?
[19:38] Maya Chen: We are SOC 2 Type II and offer SSO via SAML/Okta, RBAC, audit logs, and KMS integrations for key management. For customers needing VPC/private control plane we have Redwood Private and on-prem options. We'll share the security pack after the call.

[22:00] Jon Patel: Back to retries and idempotency: For idempotent text generation calls, include an idempotency token header. If you retry due to 5xx you'll get the same request treated once. For streaming we recommend reconnect patterns and supporting partial replay.

[24:40] Priya Rao: Any limits on stream length or timeouts?
[24:46] Jon Patel: There are platform timeouts — default session idle timeouts and max response size (varies by model). For very long streaming you should use chunked responses and checkpointing in your client. We'll share the exact limits in the docs.

[27:10] Liam O'Connor: Performance testing — can we run a short benchmark to see p99 latencies from our EU region?
[27:18] Maya Chen: Yes. We can spin up a short pilot on hosted and do benchmarks; if you need guarantees we can propose Dedicated nodes colocated in the region.

[29:00] Evan Miles: Competitors — how do you compare vs OpenAI or Anthropic for latency/cost?
[29:08] Maya Chen: High level: Redwood focuses on production economics. We give knobs for batching, caching, and quantization recommendations via Redwood Optimize. Many customers see lower unit costs for steady-state loads vs raw hosted alternatives, and Dedicated lets you lock in throughput. We'll send a benchmark spreadsheet with apples-to-apples numbers.

[31:35] Jon Patel: Quick note on retries: use exponential backoff starting at ~200-500ms, with jitter, and cap at a few seconds for interactive UIs. For background jobs you can be more aggressive. Also instrument retries so you can alert on repeated failures.

[34:50] Priya Rao: For our platform team: what does integration look like? Are there SDKs for Python/Node?
[34:55] Jon Patel: Yes, we have official SDKs for Python, Node, Go; plus REST. SDK includes streaming helpers, retry policy helpers, and helpers for idempotency tokens.

[37:00] Liam O'Connor: Any gotchas with stop sequences and streaming?
[37:05] Jon Patel: If you use stop tokens, streaming will still emit the final stop-delimited chunk. You may need to post-process to strip stop markers. Also be careful that custom stop sequences can truncate earlier than expected.

[39:20] Maya Chen: Quick recap — we covered streaming, params, retries, caching and security. We'll send pricing and the security pack.

[40:00] Evan Miles: Timeline — we're aiming to pick a provider and run a pilot within 3 weeks.
[40:07] Maya Chen: Great. We'll follow up with next steps.

[42:00] End notes: audio quality medium; some words mis-transcribed (model names, product nicknames).

Recap / Next steps spoken on call:
- Maya to share hosted vs dedicated comparison, pricing, and security pack.
- Jon to propose quick benchmark plan and a starter notebook script for streaming tests.
- Customer to confirm pilot scope and timelines (3 week target).
